source.title: Weak and Strong Gradient Directions: Explaining Memorization, Generalization, and Hardness of Examples at Scale.
source.authors: Piotr Zieliński; Shankar Krishnan; Satrajit Chatterjee

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present
record.tranche_reason: Applies label noise and measures training and test performance with SGD on ImageNet and CIFAR-10, including new model and dataset settings.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results for RM3, M3, RA3, and winsorization. These change the gradient aggregation method; rows are included where the reported outcome bears directly on fitting corrupted labels. Results cited from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study extends random-label fitting and learning-dynamics experiments to ImageNet with ResNet, Inception and VGG, and independently confirms memorization on CIFAR-10. Its own SGD results bear on V1, V2, V4 and V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors interpret the label-noise, gradient-suppression and easy/hard-example experiments as evidence for Coherent Gradients at scale. They report standard-SGD memorization and reduced memorization under suppression, and propose that shared patterns are learned first. This remains evidence for a qualitative hypothesis, rather than proof of a general mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: Uses label randomization and train/test accuracy measurements related to the original studies, but applies them to ImageNet and CIFAR-10 and adds gradient-suppression experiments. Training settings include different architectures, datasets, and schedules.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with label-noise fraction, model and dataset; suppressing weak directions with winsorization, RM3 or M3 changes fitting behavior. The authors report that RM3 behavior depends on mini-batch size and that suppression can make training less stable, particularly at low noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Winsorization prevents random-label memorization, and RM3 selectively inhibits learning corrupt examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing weak gradient directions can reduce memorization under modified training procedures.

fits_no_version.finding: A ResNet-18 initialized from a model fitted to real ImageNet labels reaches 90% random-label training accuracy in 62 epochs, versus 81 from random initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features acquired from real labels can accelerate subsequent random-label memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: Separately trained easy ImageNet examples generalize better than hard examples; hard-to-easy accuracy is 44%, versus 85% for easy-to-easy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Naturally easy and hard examples differ in generalization, challenging one interpretation of training as exploring progressively more complex decision boundaries.

record.problems: Several key accuracy results are presented only in plots, with no exact values. The authors report no error bars and say they did no hyperparameter search. For VGG, training was stopped when training accuracy reached 100%.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The study does not report numerical training-time comparisons suitable for V2, explicit-regularization comparisons for V5, or unstructured-input results for V3.

untested.parts: Exact chance-level test error is not numerically established. ImageNet experiments omit augmentation and weight decay, so they do not establish robustness to retaining those regularizers.
No matched time-to-fit comparison establishes that random labels require only a small constant factor more training than true labels. Slower learning with increasing noise is tested qualitatively.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
The exact cross-fraction progression toward chance cannot be assessed from the supplied figure text; the paper's temporal test-accuracy decline is a different comparison.
No controlled comparison of weight decay, dropout or augmentation, and no comparison establishing the generalization effect of removing them. Their omission alone does not test V5.

missing.what: Pristine-versus-corrupt learning trajectories for Inception-V3 and VGG-13. The captions explicitly confirm Section 2's learning-order predictions, but R8–R9 record only aggregate train/test curves.
missing.locator: Appendix A, Figures 6(c–d) and 7(c–d), and their captions
missing.versions: V6; also V2 for slowdown with increasing noise

record.verdict_notes: This study is neither listed original source. The supplied text omits readable plotted trajectories, so exact accuracies and cross-noise trends cannot be reconstructed. Temporal overfitting does not contradict V4's comparison across noise fractions. Modified-optimizer results do not warrant the record's V4 challenge or V6 scope limitation.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Label-noise training curves are discussed, but no numerical training-time comparison or constant-factor cost is reported.
The text does not give numerical train or test error values across every noise fraction; plotted values are retained as figure-only.
The study reports training without augmentation or weight decay, but does not test dropout, or whether removing regularizers alone harms generalization on true labels.
The paper measures pristine and corrupt examples under label noise, but does not establish a general mechanism distinguishing how real and random labels are learned.
